title: An Empirical Framework for Testing the Stress–Dominance Hypothesis: Two Adversity Gradients, Three Trait Components, and Spatial Scale
content: The Stress–Dominance Hypothesis predicts changes in functional trait dispersion along gradients of environmental and competitive adversity. However, empirical testing is complicated by issues such as null-model specification, overlapping ecological functions of traits, and the identification of adversity gradients. An empirical framework for testing these predictions in aquatic macrophyte communities was applied, combining null-model randomisation with an orthogonal decomposition of the species-by-traits matrix into environment-sensitive, competition-sensitive, and residual components. Independent indicators of environmental and competitive adversity were derived from community-level plant strategy composition, alongside spatial-scale partitioning. High environmental adversity was associated with underdispersion of environment-sensitive traits, consistent with environmental filtering, and this pattern was predominantly structured at broad spatial scales. Conversely, high competitive adversity was associated with overdispersion of competition-sensitive traits, consistent with limiting similarity under symmetric competition, with a greater contribution from finer spatial scales. Competition also generated an alternative pattern: trait convergence associated with asymmetric competition was detected in the residual trait component and exhibited substantial medium- and fine-scale structure. These results indicate that environmental and competitive adversity represent distinct dimensions of community assembly, and that their effects on functional diversity can be distinguished by combining trait decomposition, appropriate null models, and spatial information.
